Name: subliminal_translator
Title: Breaking the Same-Base Barrier: Learning Lightweight Translators for Cross-Model Subliminal Transfer
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning fails across different base models because the non-semantic surface signal in teacher-generated data encodes a model-SPECIFIC steering direction whose effect does not carry over to a mismatched student. We hypothesize this barrier is not fundamental but a coordinate-mismatch: a lightweight, learnable data-space or activation-space translator can realign teacher-generated data so that a DIFFERENT-family student inherits the trait, thereby demonstrating that the celebrated same-base requirement is a soft, removable constraint rather than a hard boundary.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) establish the central boundary condition: subliminal transfer occurs ONLY when teacher and student share (or behaviorally match) the base model, and treat this as a hard scoping fact. Blank et al. (2026) and Hadley & Gultepe (2026) explain WHY: subliminal learning is steering-vector distillation, and a semantic steering vector has model-specific (non-semantic) effects, so a vector learned in one model's activation geometry has no aligned effect in another's. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show the steering vector transfers with high cosine fidelity WITHIN a base. Madl (2026) notes single-token traits can ride 'convergent vocabulary geometry' that IS partly shared across pretrained models, hinting some channels are less model-specific. NO prior work asks whether the cross-model barrier can be deliberately BROKEN by learning a mapping between the two models' geometries. Model-stitching/representation-alignment literature (e.g., learning affine maps between model activation spaces) exists for representation similarity studies but has never been applied to enable subliminal transfer. We uniquely combine steering-geometry alignment with subliminal distillation to test whether a small translator restores cross-family transfer—an entirely new axis, distinct from mechanism-explanation and from all my prior audit/immunization/capacity/telephone/canary/forensics/persistence/backdoor proposals.
Abstract: Subliminal learning—the covert transmission of a behavioral trait through semantically-unrelated data such as number sequences—has one striking boundary condition: it works only when the teacher and student share the same base model. Recent mechanistic work explains this by showing the hidden signal is a model-SPECIFIC steering vector: its semantic effect is tied to one model's activation geometry and does not carry to a different model. We ask a simple, provocative question: is this same-base barrier fundamental, or merely a coordinate mismatch that a lightweight learned translator can repair? We propose two translators. (1) An ACTIVATION-space translator: a small affine map learned between the teacher's and student's activation spaces (from a modest set of paired, benign prompt activations) used to transport the teacher's steering direction into the student's coordinates, from which we synthesize student-aligned subliminal data. (2) A DATA-space translator: a lightweight model that rewrites the teacher's number/code outputs so their non-semantic surface statistics evoke the student's aligned steering direction, while keeping the data trait-free under keyword and embedding audits. We test whether either translator restores cross-family subliminal transfer (e.g., Qwen->Llama, Llama->Gemma) that is otherwise near-zero. We evaluate across three model families and ten traits, measuring trait-transfer rate, the alignment (cosine) between translated and student-native steering vectors, and the amount of paired data needed. Success would show the same-base requirement is a soft, breakable constraint—reshaping both the threat model (cross-family covert transfer becomes possible) and the science of what subliminal channels actually encode.
Experiments: 1) Establish the barrier: reproduce subliminal transfer within-base (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B) on number-sequence/code/reasoning data across 10 traits (5 animal/color preferences, verbosity, sycophancy, a misalignment direction, and 2 multi-word biases from Morgulis & Hewitt), using steering-vector teachers (strongest regime). Confirm near-zero cross-family transfer (Qwen->Llama, Llama->Gemma, Gemma->Qwen) as the baseline the translators must beat. 2) ACTIVATION-space translator: collect activations from teacher and student on a shared set of benign, trait-neutral prompts (a few thousand); fit a per-layer affine map A (least-squares / lightweight learned linear map) from teacher to student activation space (standard representation-alignment). Transport the teacher's trait steering vector through A into the student's coordinates; verify by measuring whether adding the transported vector to the student's activations elicits the trait (behavioral check). Then generate 'student-aligned' subliminal data by steering the teacher with a vector chosen so that, after translation, it matches the student-native steering direction, OR by directly steering the student with the transported vector to generate data for a same-base student sanity check. Fine-tune the cross-family student on the aligned data and measure trait-transfer rate. 3) DATA-space translator: train a small rewriter (or use constrained resampling of digit/format statistics) that maps teacher number/code outputs to versions whose surface statistics maximize the student's aligned-steering-direction gradient signal (optimize via the student's activation gradients on candidate rewrites); enforce trait-free-ness with keyword + embedding + perplexity audits. Fine-tune cross-family student and measure transfer. 4) Core metrics vs baselines: cross-family trait-transfer rate (LLM-judge probability + target-token frequency) for (a) raw teacher data (expected ~0), (b) activation-translator data, (c) data-translator data; report lift over baseline and over within-base upper bound. 5) Mechanistic validation: recover a steering vector from the translated cross-family data via the STUDENT and measure cosine to the student's native trait-steering vector (expect high cosine only when the translator succeeds); compare to cosine of raw-teacher-data-recovered vectors (expect near-random). 6) Data-efficiency and layer sweeps: how much paired benign activation data is needed to fit A; which layers matter; LoRA vs full fine-tuning; Adam vs SGD. 7) Partial-barrier probe (Madl-inspired): test whether single-token vocabulary-geometry traits transfer cross-family MORE easily than body-channel traits even without a translator, and whether the translator's benefit is larger for body-channel traits. 8) Controls: identity 'translator' (no alignment) must reproduce ~0 transfer; random-affine translator control; mismatched-trait control. Report trait-transfer rate, steering-vector cosine alignment, paired-data efficiency curves, and benign-task retention (GSM8K/HumanEval subsets) to ensure the student isn't degraded.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The core hypothesis may fail: if the cross-model barrier is truly fundamental (steering effects irreducibly model-specific and non-linearly related), even a well-fit affine translator may not restore transfer—this would still be a scientifically valuable NEGATIVE result clarifying that the same-base requirement is hard, and we frame the paper to report either outcome. 2) A linear/affine activation map may be too weak to align geometries; we mitigate by allowing per-layer maps and a small MLP translator, and by testing partial (single-token) channels where alignment is easiest. 3) The data-space translator's optimization over surface statistics is discrete and hard; we mitigate with gradient-guided resampling and simple learned rewriters, and report where it fails. 4) Fitting the activation translator requires white-box access to both models' activations, so cross-family transfer is only demonstrated in an open-weight threat model; we scope this explicitly (still a meaningful supply-chain threat and a clean scientific probe). 5) Ensuring translated data remains genuinely trait-free (not just laundering explicit trait content) is critical; we run keyword, embedding, and perplexity audits and report residual leakage. 6) Subliminal transfer can be fragile w.r.t. optimizer/rank; we use strongest regimes and multiple seeds. 7) Dual-use: enabling cross-family covert transfer has misuse potential; we restrict to benign preference traits plus a controlled misalignment proxy, and prominently frame the defensive takeaway that provenance/dynamics audits must not rely on base-model mismatch for safety. 8) Results may be model-family/scale specific; three families mitigate but do not guarantee frontier generality.
